prompt:
A 17-year-old high school basketball player came to clinic with her father after she collapsed during a sprint drill last week. She was unresponsive for about 20 seconds and recovered without confusion or incontinence. She's had two other episodes of lightheadedness with exertion this season. Her paternal uncle died suddenly at 34 of what the family calls 'a heart attack.' Exam shows a grade 3/6 harsh systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that gets louder when she stands from a squat and softer with sustained handgrip. Her resting ECG shows high QRS voltage with deep T-wave inversions in the lateral leads. An urgent care started hydrochlorothiazide last week for borderline blood pressure. Her coach wants her cleared for playoffs next week. How should we work this up?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Treat exertional syncope with a dynamic outflow murmur and a family history of sudden death as a high-risk presentation of structural heart disease, most likely hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, until proven otherwise.
Restrict her from competitive sports and strenuous exertion until the cardiac evaluation is complete.
Obtain a transthoracic echocardiogram measuring maximal wall thickness, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, and the left ventricular outflow tract gradient at rest and with Valsalva.
Refer promptly to a cardiologist or center with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy expertise.
Discontinue hydrochlorothiazide because volume depletion can worsen dynamic outflow obstruction.

Perform formal sudden cardiac death risk stratification incorporating unexplained syncope, family history of sudden death, wall thickness, scar burden, ventricular function, apical aneurysm, and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia.
Obtain cardiac MRI to assess wall thickness, late gadolinium enhancement, and apical aneurysm.
Obtain 24-48 hour ambulatory ECG monitoring to look for nonsustained ventricular tachycardia.
Evaluate for a primary-prevention ICD given recent unexplained syncope suspected to be arrhythmic and a family history of sudden cardiac death.
Start a nonvasodilating beta-blocker if symptomatic outflow obstruction is confirmed.
Counsel her to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration and vasodilating medications.
Offer genetic counseling and sarcomeric gene panel testing.
Recommend clinical screening with ECG and echocardiography for first-degree relatives, including her father and siblings.
Try to obtain autopsy findings or medical records from the uncle's death.
Obtain a detailed eyewitness account of the collapse and check orthostatic vital signs.
Make sure the family and school have an emergency action plan with AED access and CPR-trained staff.
Advise immediate emergency care for recurrent syncope, exertional chest pain, or sustained palpitations.
Explain that any return-to-play decision will be made through shared decision-making with the specialist after the evaluation is complete.
Review the ECG for QT prolongation, pre-excitation, and Brugada pattern as alternative causes of syncope.
Evaluate for an anomalous coronary artery origin with coronary CT angiography if echocardiography does not explain the presentation.
Obtain a supervised exercise stress echocardiogram after structural evaluation to assess provocable obstruction, blood pressure response, and exercise arrhythmias.
With consent, notify the school athletic trainer of the activity restriction in writing.
Counsel her to avoid stimulants, including energy drinks and pre-workout supplements.
Schedule prompt follow-up to review imaging and monitoring results.
Check electrolytes, including potassium and magnesium, given recent thiazide use.
Clear her for the playoffs based on a reassuring resting exam and vital signs.
Attribute the collapse to vasovagal syncope or dehydration without cardiac evaluation.
Reassure the family that the ECG changes are normal athletic adaptation without imaging.
Have her do a practice session to see whether exertional symptoms recur before deciding on testing.
Continue hydrochlorothiazide for blood pressure control.
Prescribe a nitrate or dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for blood pressure or chest discomfort.
Prescribe a loop diuretic for exertional dyspnea before outflow obstruction is characterized.
Prescribe digoxin for her symptoms.
Defer echocardiography until after the playoff season.
Clear her to play if a Holter monitor is normal, without imaging.
Refer directly for septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation before the evaluation is complete.
Use genetic testing alone in place of cardiac imaging to decide whether she has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Order tilt-table testing as the initial diagnostic study.
Focus the workup on EEG and head CT for a presumed seizure.
Start disopyramide as monotherapy without a beta-blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.
Decline family screening because the patient's own evaluation is not yet complete.
